Steps.Title: Eligible devices are onboarded to Defender for Endpoint
Steps.Summary: Every device that Defender for Endpoint can protect reports to it through a working sensor, so the device has a risk level.
Rollout: Assign an Intune EDR onboarding policy to a test device group, and check that the devices appear in the Defender portal's device inventory.
Then assign it to all Windows devices.
Deploy the Defender app to macOS, Android and iOS/iPadOS devices, which have no automatic onboarding package.
Steps.Unchecked: No Maester check yet. The Zero Trust Assessment pack checks it (ZTA.41045) once its results can name steps.

Sources.Note: Onboarding Windows devices through Intune lists the Intune connection as a prerequisite.
With the connection, Intune gets Defender's onboarding package for its EDR policy. Without it, you paste an onboarding package into the policy yourself.

Steps.Title: Publish an SPF record for every domain that sends mail
Steps.Summary: Receiving servers can check that mail from your domains comes from Microsoft 365 or another sender you list.
Rollout: List every system that sends as the domain: Microsoft 365, on-premises servers and third-party services.
Publish one SPF TXT record per sending domain and subdomain, and keep it under ten DNS lookups.
Give domains that never send mail the record v=spf1 -all.

Sources.Note: Each custom domain and sending subdomain needs one SPF TXT record naming Microsoft 365 and any other senders. onmicrosoft.com is covered already.

Steps.Title: End every SPF record with -all
Steps.Summary: Receivers are told to reject mail from servers that the SPF record doesn't list, so DMARC can act on spoofed mail with no signature.
Rollout: Keep ~all until the DMARC aggregate reports show no legitimate source failing SPF.
Change the qualifier to -all one domain at a time, keeping one SPF record per domain.

Sources.Note: Start with the senders you know and ~all, add the others as you find them, then move to -all, so mail from a sender you missed isn't bounced.
DMARC reports show which servers send as the domain, so publish a DMARC record early and read its reports before -all rejects a source nobody listed.

Steps.Title: Sign outbound mail with DKIM for every custom domain
Steps.Summary: Mail from your custom domains carries a DKIM signature that matches the From domain and survives forwarding.
Rollout: Read the two CNAME values for the domain from the Defender portal or Get-DkimSigningConfig.
Create both selector CNAME records at the DNS host and wait until Microsoft 365 detects them.
Turn on DKIM signing for the domain and confirm that its status shows it is signing.

Sources.Note: Custom domains aren't signed until both selector CNAME records exist and signing is on. onmicrosoft.com is signed already, and parked domains need no DKIM.

Steps.Title: Publish a DMARC record for every domain
Steps.Summary: Every domain, onmicrosoft.com included, has a DMARC record, so receivers check alignment and report who sends mail as you.
Rollout: Publish v=DMARC1; p=none with a rua address that a dedicated mailbox or a reporting service reads.
Add the record for the onmicrosoft.com domain in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
Read the aggregate reports regularly to find senders that fail SPF or DKIM.

Sources.Note: Set up SPF and DKIM before DMARC, which passes only on aligned SPF or DKIM. A p=none record changes no delivery and starts the reports.
The onmicrosoft.com domain needs a DMARC record of its own, added in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Steps.Title: Enforce DMARC with reporting on every domain
Steps.Summary: Receivers quarantine or reject mail that fails DMARC for any of your domains, and send you aggregate and failure reports.
Rollout: Start with a low-volume domain or subdomain, and leave the parent domain for last.
Move from p=none to p=quarantine, and raise pct in steps from 10 to 100 while you watch the reports.
Keep the rua and ruf addresses in the record so that failures go on being reported.

Sources.Note: An enforcing policy acts on mail that fails both aligned SPF and DKIM. Set both up on every sending domain first, and run p=none with reports before you enforce.
The deployment guide sets up SPF, DKIM and DMARC in that order, and expects quarantine or reject with report addresses on each custom domain.
With ~all, DMARC in effect ignores SPF failures on mail that has no DKIM signature. Ending SPF in -all lets the policy act on that mail.

Steps.Title: Reject mail that fails DMARC on every domain
Steps.Summary: Receivers reject mail that claims to come from your domains but fails DMARC, parked domains and onmicrosoft.com included.
Rollout: After a period at p=quarantine, move each domain to p=reject, raising pct in steps if needed.
Do the subdomains in order of volume, then the parent domain.
Set parked domains and an unused onmicrosoft.com domain to p=reject straight away.

Sources.Note: The target is p=reject on every domain, reached after a period at quarantine. Parked domains and an onmicrosoft.com domain that sends nothing can go straight there.
